hook: Some Chinese porcelain took as many as 72 steps to make, often by a team of craftsmen working together.
lede: A maker working alone must still master every core stage, from throwing and molding to glazing and firing, and the digital tools that could cut some of those steps ask for CAD and CAM skills many ceramic makers lack. We built a workflow in which generative AI turns a rough sketch and a few words into a textured 3D model, a clay printer builds it with the pattern engraved into its surface, and the maker glazes by following those lines. Four ceramic creators then used it to make their own pieces, and told us what it gave them and what it took away.

chapters.title: Two authors, each holding half the process
paragraphs: The workflow began with two of us, the paper’s co-first authors: Author A, a design researcher who works with GenAI tools for creative support, and Author B, a ceramic artist who specializes in clay 3D printing. A showed B how current tools generate design images and 3D models; B walked A through the traditional ceramic-making process and the state of clay printing.

From minimal line sketches and short descriptions, A generated images of textured Chinese ceramic forms, then 3D models and UV textures. B judged that the forms and motifs fit established Chinese ceramic aesthetics and were good enough to guide fabrication.

It set him thinking about which steps of the craft AI could support. Hand sketches usually stay bare outlines, because drawing patterns and colors takes time; craftspeople often put off complete drawings until they are waiting for clay to dry or a kiln to fire. Complex forms demand repeated practice, and freehand decoration demands accumulated experience. He saw a role for AI at each stage: renderings straight from a simple sketch, base forms generated for printing, and patterns engraved into the surface to guide the glaze.

figures.caption: The three designs Author A presented to Author B, each as sketch, generated image and 3D model: a lattice screen with Chinese motifs, a baozi-shaped sculpture and a Tang Sancai jar with dragon relief.

chapters.title: Where the clay gave way
paragraphs: A guided the model with visual references B selected, such as Qinghua brush motifs and Tang sancai glaze palettes, and produced five designs, from a traditional Qing Hua vase to a checkerboard jar. B engraved their patterns into the models in Rhino and Grasshopper, adjusting the depth so the motifs would stay legible after firing and still support glazing.

Printing was where the designs met their limits. Steep overhangs and thin structures often collapsed. For the Checkerboard Jar, Grasshopper’s structural analysis marked the neck in red, and the print collapsed at the same place. Not every model could be printed, and some generated patterns were too vague to engrave cleanly.

After multiple trials, B printed the Qing Hua vase at two engraving depths, filled the lines with glaze and sponged off the excess; both vases were finished. The trials left rules for the tool that followed.
points: Keep slopes under 45° and avoid thin structures.
Engrave 1–1.5 mm deep to guide glaze, allowing for wall thickness.
Pair text prompts with sketches and visual references, and prefer patterns with clean outlines.

figures.caption: AI-generated UV textures (top) and the same patterns engraved by Author B into the models (bottom).

chapters.title: Guides, not molds
paragraphs: ClayScape folds these lessons into three connected workspaces. In the prompt area, a creator can type a description, draw or upload a sketch, and pick a decorative style, color and level of detail. Shape templates, simplified from vessels in the Palace Museum’s collection and adjusted for clay printing, act as optional structural guides rather than fixed molds; pattern styles draw on black-and-white porcelain, Tang tri-color (Sancai) and Qinghua.

A 3D preview lets the creator turn the model through 360° and regenerate its texture. A print preview exposes Pattern Depth, Line Thickness and Print Speed, estimates print time and clay use, and exports G-code for the printer.

figures.caption: ClayScape’s three workspaces: (a) prompt area, (b) 3D design preview and (c) clay print preview with G-code export.
Motifs Author B introduced in Phase 1 (left) and the matching pattern styles in ClayScape (right).

chapters.title: Forms they could not finish by hand
paragraphs: Four creators took part: two beginners with less than a year of ceramic experience and two advanced artists with five or more years. None had combined GenAI with ceramics or clay printing. Each designed a piece in ClayScape while thinking aloud, then, once the print had dried, glazed it in Author B’s studio.

A01 wanted forms she could not finish by hand and patterns she could not draw herself. She engraved crackle textures into a bowl; the glaze did not produce a true crackle, but the engraved textures worked convincingly. A02, who lacked confidence in drawing floral motifs, regenerated her vase from round to square to octagonal, chose the octagon for its resonance with Chinese aesthetics, and glazed it by following the engraving. “Now, in less than two hours, we already finished all the glazing,” she said.

For A03, an experienced artist, the tool’s unpredictability became a source of ideas: the first version generated from her sculpture sketch, a “pudding-shaped” form, suggested a Chinese-style candle warmer, a direction she had not considered before.

quote.text: My hand-drawn lines often look shaky, making the vessel seem irregular. But after the AI processed it, that randomness and irregularity were preserved as a solid effect.

figures.caption: A02’s vase, from sketch and prompt through rounded, quadrilateral and octagonal variants to the print, texture-guided glazing and the fired piece.

chapters.title: A hole that was not reasonable
paragraphs: The printed surface resisted the glaze: thin layers left small gaps, engraved textures added roughness, and the beginners found it hard to glaze evenly. Despite the templates and print preview, some pieces still printed with minor collapses, and A01’s bowl came out with an unexpected hole in its wall. She usually embraced randomness, but not this.

The experienced artists pushed against the limits on purpose. A04 wanted challenging forms rather than simple, boring ones, and Author B had to step in, removing the sharp lid from A03’s candle warmer and adding support to the handle of A04’s vessel. That help led A04 back to the problem the workflow set out to solve: “creators must be equipped with CAM skills and knowledge of structural feasibility in clay print. So it is still limited.”

A03 met a subtler limit. Her candle warmer’s hollow was very small, and she doubted a candle would fit; by hand she could have adjusted it easily, but ClayScape could not yet control that level of detail.

quote.text: I really like the randomness of creation, AI generation and clay print both have it. For example, when printing a head, the collapsed clay might look like hair, which is reasonable. But this hole was not reasonable.

figures.caption: Where printing fell short: (A) collapsed layers, (B) the hole in A01’s bowl, (C) added support for A04’s handle and (D) the sharp lid removed from A03’s candle warmer.

chapters.title: From shaping a work to influencing it
paragraphs: The guides that made the work easier also, at times, hemmed it in. Some generated forms felt too regular to the beginners, and A02 felt that making rough, spontaneous ideas too concrete drained them: “Making them too concrete takes away their wild beauty.” The engraved lines told A01 where to apply color, though during glazing she sometimes had new ideas; she proposed engraving at varied depths, and A02 suggested removable stickers.

A04 took his own route. From stories of old ceramic objects he had collected, he chose a vase once used as a family coin container, then glazed it closer to his own imagination rather than relying only on the generated design, working with the printed texture: “I wanted to see how I could use this uneven surface to enhance the effect.” The piece came out resembling an aged ceramic object.

For A01, the difference lay in the clay: an AI-generated image alone would not have felt like hers, but once she knew it could become a real piece, she started to feel anticipation. We had expected ClayScape and clay printing to replace some traditional steps; our findings suggested they work better as assistants, and A04, skilled in both hand-building and clay printing, emphasized that neither should replace the other. A01 put the shift this way: “In traditional craft, I felt I was shaping a work from 0 to 1. Now it feels like influencing from 1 to 2.”

quote.text: It’s kind of taking away the quality of the painting. You’re tracing a pattern, but it’s still not a painting. It’s a generated painting, a secondary painting.

figures.caption: A04’s money jar, from a sketch drawn from a family memory to the generated design, the print, hand-glazing and a fired piece resembling an aged ceramic object.

takeaways: Generative AI and clay printing support each other: AI lowers the barrier to digital fabrication, and printing makes AI designs real enough to sustain a maker’s engagement.
Beginners found entry points into forms and patterns beyond their hands, while experienced artists questioned how such workflows should be balanced with traditional craft skills.
Hybrid tools work better as assistants than substitutes: guides help, but makers need room to depart from them, and complex forms still call for craft and CAM knowledge.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: Two-phase study informed by participatory design and research through design

facts.label: Phase 1
facts.value: The co-first authors, a GenAI design researcher and a ceramic artist in clay 3D printing, co-created the workflow

facts.label: Phase 2
facts.value: 4 creators (2 beginners, 2 advanced artists); co-design and glazing sessions, each followed by a ~30-minute interview

facts.label: Phase 1 tools
facts.value: Text-to-image multimodal LLMs, Tripo, Meshy, Rhino and Grasshopper

facts.label: Limitations
facts.value: Layer lines, overhang limits and air pockets; users still need prompting, printing and glazing basics; less granular control over form
